questions.q: Electric current is the movement of charged particles, yet the textbook says random motion of electrons in a metal conductor is not an electric current. Why not?
options: The electrons are moving too slowly to count as a current
There is no net movement of charge in one direction, since the electrons move in random directions
Electrons are negative, so they cannot carry a current
A metal conductor has no charged particles that are free to move
questions.explanation: For a current to exist there must be a net movement of charge in one direction. In a piece of metal conductor the electrons are constantly moving in random directions, so there is no net movement in one direction and no current. A battery supplies the field that drives that net drift.

questions.q: What is the current in a conductor if 10 coulombs of charge pass a point in 5.0 seconds?
questions.explanation: Current is charge per time, \(I = Q/t\). Ten coulombs passing a point in 5.0 seconds gives 2.0 coulombs per second, which is 2.0 amperes.

questions.q: The textbook explains the meaning of the ampere in terms of electrons. When the current is 1 ampere, how many electrons pass through a cross-section of the conductor in one second?
options: 1 electron
6.25 × 10¹⁸ electrons
1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ electrons
6.0 × 10²³ electrons
questions.explanation: One coulomb is equivalent to 6.25 × 10¹⁸ electrons, so when the current is 1 ampere that many electrons pass through a cross-section of the conductor each second. A current of 5.00 A for 6.00 s therefore moves 1.88 × 10²⁰ electrons.

questions.q: Distinguish conventional current from electron current in a metal conductor, as described in the textbook.
options: Conventional current and electron current both flow from the negative terminal to the positive terminal
Conventional current is taken as positive charge moving from the positive terminal to the negative terminal, while the electron charge carriers in a metal conductor actually move the opposite way
Conventional current is the movement of electrons; electron current is the movement of positive ions
There is no difference; the two terms describe the same direction of flow
questions.explanation: Before the electron was known, current was accepted as the movement of positive charge leaving the positive terminal and travelling to the negative terminal — this is conventional current. In reality the charge carriers in a metal conductor are electrons, which move the opposite way.

questions.q: From memory: what does the potential difference V across a power supply measure, and what equation defines it?
keyPoints: The potential difference V is a measure of the number of joules of electric potential energy given to each coulomb of charge that passes through it.
For example, a 5-volt battery gives 5 joules of electric potential energy to each coulomb of charge.
It is defined by \(V = \dfrac{W}{q}\), and is measured in volts (1 volt = 1 joule per coulomb).
questions.explanation: If you recalled that potential difference is energy per coulomb of charge and stated V = W/q, grade yourself Good or Easy. The textbook's worked example: a 5-volt supply gives 5 joules to every coulomb.

questions.q: Calculate the amount of electric potential energy given to 2.00 coulomb of charge that passes through a 1.50 × 10² V power supply.
questions.explanation: Potential difference is energy per charge, V = W/q, so the energy given to the charge is W = Vq. A 150 V supply gives 150 joules to each coulomb, so 2.00 coulomb receive 300 joules.

questions.q: The textbook defines resistance by the equation R = V/I, but warns that this is not Ohm's Law unless a condition is met. What is that condition?
options: The current must be measured in milliamperes
R must be constant — the V versus I graph is not a straight line for a metallic conductor unless the temperature is constant
The voltage drop must be exactly one volt
The conductor must be a semiconductor
questions.explanation: R = V/I always defines resistance, but it is only Ohm's Law when R is constant. For a metallic conductor the V versus I graph is a straight line only if the temperature is held constant; otherwise the resistance changes.

questions.q: According to the textbook, what distinguishes an ohmic device from a non-ohmic device?
options: An ohmic device has zero resistance; a non-ohmic device has infinite resistance

An ohmic device has constant resistance for all currents under constant physical conditions such as temperature, while a non-ohmic device has a different resistance for different currents passing through it
An ohmic device works only with alternating current; a non-ohmic device only with direct current
An ohmic device is made of a semiconductor; a non-ohmic device is made of metal
questions.explanation: An ohmic device is one for which, under constant physical conditions such as temperature, the resistance is constant for all currents that pass through it. A non-ohmic device, such as a diode, has a resistance that is different for different currents.

questions.q: What is the power rating of an electric heater if a current of 5.0 A flows through it when there is a voltage drop of 240 V across the heating element?
questions.explanation: Power is voltage times current, P = VI. With a voltage drop of 240 V across the heating element and a current of 5.0 A, the power rating is 1200 W, or 1.2 kW.

questions.q: The textbook states the resistance of a particular conductor is determined by four factors. Which set correctly lists those four factors?
options: Length, material, area of cross-section, temperature
Charge, voltage, current, power
Mass, density, colour, length
Voltage drop, current, time, energy
questions.explanation: Resistance arises from collisions between free electrons and the lattice of positive ions, and the four factors that determine it are length, material, area of cross-section and temperature. A longer or thinner conductor, a higher-resistivity material, or a hotter conductor all raise the resistance.

questions.q: Explain, using a current–voltage graph, why a filament lamp is a non-ohmic component. (4 marks)
questions.modelAnswer: As the voltage across a filament lamp, and hence the current through it, increases, the filament gets hotter. In a metal, a higher temperature means a higher resistance, because the more vigorously vibrating atoms impede the flow of electrons more. So as the voltage rises the resistance rises too, and the current increases by less and less for each extra volt. On a current-versus-voltage graph this appears as a line that curves and flattens, rather than the straight line of an ohmic conductor. Because the resistance is not constant, Ohm's Law does not apply, so the filament lamp is non-ohmic.

criteria.descriptor: States that increasing current heats the filament.
States that a higher temperature gives a higher resistance in the metal filament.
Describes the I–V graph as a curve that flattens, not a straight line.
Concludes the resistance is not constant, so it is non-ohmic / Ohm's Law does not apply.

questions.explanation: The marks reward the causal chain: more current heats the filament, higher temperature raises resistance, the I–V graph curves, and non-constant resistance means non-ohmic. 'The lamp doesn't obey Ohm's Law' just restates the question.

questions.q: Two heating elements, A (12 Ω) and B (24 Ω), are each connected, one at a time, across the same 240 V supply. Which element dissipates more power, and why?
options: Element B, because its higher resistance dissipates more power at fixed voltage
Element A, because at fixed voltage power is V²/R, so the lower resistance dissipates more power
Both dissipate equal power, because they share the same supply voltage
Element A, because a higher resistance always draws a larger current
questions.explanation: With the voltage fixed, the direct form is P = V²/R. Element A: 240²/12 = 4800 W; element B: 240²/24 = 2400 W. At fixed voltage power is inversely proportional to resistance, so the lower-resistance element A dissipates more power.
